text: Before dawn on 6 August 2024 Ukrainian regular brigades crossed the border into Kursk Oblast.
Ukraine prepared the Kursk incursion over a long period: Ukrainian special forces had worked in the Russian rear since June 2024.
A company of the 80th Air Assault Brigade had hidden in border forests in Kursk Oblast since 4 August 2024, before the main crossing.
Russian communications and surveillance were suppressed before the Ukrainian crossing into Kursk Oblast on 6 August 2024.
The Ukrainian build-up in Sumy Oblast before the Kursk incursion passed as a defensive deployment.

The 80th and 82nd Air Assault and 22nd Mechanised brigades broke a thin Russian line of conscripts, FSB border guards and Akhmat units on two axes, from the Sudzha checkpoint and from Novenke, on 6 August 2024.
Within a day of the 6 August 2024 break-in, Ukrainian forces held the Sudzha border checkpoint.
By Russian accounts, Ukrainian forces held the Sudzha gas distribution (metering) station within a day of the 6 August 2024 break-in.
By 14–15 August 2024 Ukrainian forces held the town of Sudzha.
From 16 to 19 August 2024 air strikes and HIMARS dropped the three Seim road bridges in Glushkovo Raion.

text: Dropping the three Seim road bridges in August 2024 isolated the Russian troops between the Seim and the border in Glushkovo Raion.
The Ukrainian advance in Kursk Oblast peaked in late August 2024 at a claimed 1,250–1,300 km².
After its late-August 2024 peak the Ukrainian advance in Kursk Oblast turned into a positional defence.
Russia began counterattacking in Kursk Oblast from 10 September 2024.
From November 2024 about 11,000–12,000 North Korean troops joined the Russian counterattack in Kursk Oblast.

text: The Kursk salient hung on one road: the H-07 from Sumy through Yunakivka to the Sudzha border crossing, which becomes the 38K-004 / R-200 in Russia.
